"Effective immediately, JPMorgan Chase is guaranteeing the trading obligations of Bear Stearns and its subsidiaries and is providing management oversight for its operations," said a statement released Sunday by JPMorgan. Shareholders must approve the deal, which is expected to close by the end of June. JPMorgan is taking immediate responsibility for Bear's trading obligations and assuming "management oversight" of the firm's operations. The deal has already been approved by the Federal Reserve and other regulators, according to the statement. The Fed is providing special emergency financing for up to $30 billion in Bear Stearns assets. "JPMorgan stands behind Bear Stearns," said Jamie Dimon, chairman and chief executive of JPMorgan. "Bear Stearns clients and counterparties should feel secure that JPMorgan is guaranteeing ... risk," he continued. The fast-track deal is expected to close by the end of June, the statement said. Bear Stearns was on the brink of financial collapse Friday when JPMorgan and the Federal Reserve Bank of New York said they would provide the brokerage a short-term loan. Bear was dealing with a classic "run on the bank." The firm's short-term creditors refused to lend the firm any more money and simultaneously demanded repayment of outstanding debt. The one-two punch overwhelmed Bear's cash position. With the global credit crisis worsening, the Fed -- along with officials from the Treasury Department and other government agencies -- took the dramatic action to prevent the investment bank from going under and igniting widespread panic through the financial markets. He would not say what might have happened had the government failed to step in. "I'm not going to speculate about what-ifs," he said. "I'm just going to say our clear priority right now -- our number one priority, everything we're doing in the economic arena -- is to minimize instability, minimize spillover into the real economy." Bear Stearns has approximately 14,000 employees worldwide. Rumors that Bear Stearns was on the verge of collapse started buzzing around Wall Street trading desks last Monday. Chief Executive Alan Schwartz -- who took over as CEO in early January from longtime chief Jimmy Cayne -- appeared on television on Wednesday afternoon to reassure the markets that the firm was stable. But by Thursday night, Bear was in a severe crunch. Some firms that trade with it effectively stopped offering it credit because they feared that Bear was running short of short-term funding, or liquidity. "The past week has been an incredibly difficult time for Bear Stearns," said Alan Schwartz, president and CEO of Bear Stearns. "This transaction represents the best outcome for all of our constituencies based upon the current circumstances." White House spokesman Tony Fratto told CNN on Sunday that Paulson has briefed U.S. President George W. Bush on the Federal Reserve's role in helping to facilitate the purchase. "We appreciate the actions taken by the Federal Reserve this evening," said Fratto. "Secretary Paulson and Chairman Bernanke are actively engaged in addressing issues affecting our financial markets. Secretary Paulson has kept the President briefed on recent developments." Shares of Bear Stearns opened last week at $69.75 and traded as high as $159 last year. E-mail to a friend .

NEW YORK (CNNMoney.com) -- JPMorgan Chase & Co. announced Sunday that it is acquiring troubled Wall Street firm Bear Stearns, amid mounting fears that Bear’s collapse could have sent shockwaves through already fragile financial markets.

The transaction to acquire Bear Stearns is valued at an estimated $236 million, or just $2 per share. Bear Stearns shares had closed at $30 on Friday, after falling 47 percent that day.

“Effective immediately, JPMorgan Chase is guaranteeing the trading obligations of Bear Stearns and its subsidiaries and is providing management oversight for its operations,” JPMorgan said in a statement released Sunday.

The deal, which must be approved by shareholders, is expected to close by the end of June. JPMorgan is assuming immediate responsibility for Bear Stearns’ trading obligations and taking “management oversight” of the firm’s operations. According to the statement, the transaction has already been approved by the Federal Reserve and other regulators.

The Federal Reserve is providing special emergency financing for up to $30 billion in Bear Stearns assets.

“JPMorgan stands behind Bear Stearns,” said Jamie Dimon, chairman and chief executive of JPMorgan. “Bear Stearns clients and counterparties should feel secure that JPMorgan is guaranteeing ... risk,” he added.

The fast-track transaction is expected to close by the end of June, the statement said.

Bear Stearns was on the brink of financial collapse Friday when JPMorgan and the Federal Reserve Bank of New York said they would provide the brokerage with a short-term loan.

The firm was facing a classic “run on the bank.” Its short-term creditors refused to lend it additional money and, at the same time, demanded repayment of outstanding debt. That one-two punch overwhelmed Bear Stearns’ cash position.

With the global credit crisis worsening, the Federal Reserve—along with officials from the Treasury Department and other government agencies—took dramatic action to prevent the investment bank from failing and triggering widespread panic across financial markets.

Watch a discussion on the impact on global markets »

Treasury Secretary Henry Paulson said Sunday that discussions over how to rescue Bear Stearns had continued throughout the weekend. He defended the Fed’s bailout on Friday as “the right decision” and said the Bush administration was prepared to take additional steps to restore stability to the financial markets.

Paulson declined to say what might have happened had the government failed to intervene.

“I’m not going to speculate about what-ifs,” he said. “I’m just going to say our clear priority right now—our number one priority, everything we’re doing in the economic arena—is to minimize instability, minimize spillover into the real economy.”

Bear Stearns has approximately 14,000 employees worldwide.

The deal marks an inglorious chapter for 85-year-old Bear Stearns, a storied Wall Street firm whose unraveling has been swift and severe.

Rumors that Bear Stearns was on the verge of collapse began circulating around Wall Street trading desks last Monday. Chief Executive Alan Schwartz, who took over in early January from longtime CEO Jimmy Cayne, appeared on television Wednesday afternoon to reassure markets that the firm was stable.

By Thursday night, however, Bear Stearns was facing a severe liquidity crunch. Some firms that traded with it effectively stopped extending credit, fearing that Bear was running short of short-term funding, or liquidity.

“The past week has been an incredibly difficult time for Bear Stearns,” said Alan Schwartz, president and CEO of Bear Stearns. “This transaction represents the best outcome for all of our constituencies based upon the current circumstances.”

White House spokesman Tony Fratto told CNN on Sunday that Paulson had briefed U.S. President George W. Bush on the Federal Reserve’s role in helping facilitate the purchase.

“We appreciate the actions taken by the Federal Reserve this evening,” Fratto said. “Secretary Paulson and Chairman Bernanke are actively engaged in addressing issues affecting our financial markets. Secretary Paulson has kept the President briefed on recent developments.”

Shares of Bear Stearns opened last week at $69.75 and traded as high as $159 last year.

**Bear Stearns Shareholders Approve Emergency Sale to JPMorgan Chase After Fed-Backed Rescue**

**NEW YORK, May 29, 2008** — Bear Stearns Cos. shareholders approved the investment bank’s emergency sale to JPMorgan Chase & Co. on Thursday, formally ending the 85-year history of one of Wall Street’s most aggressive firms and closing a dramatic chapter in the credit crisis that shook global financial markets.

The vote capped a stunning collapse for Bear Stearns, which only months earlier had been one of the largest U.S. securities firms. The company was forced into a rescue sale in March after a sudden run on its liquidity left it unable to fund day-to-day operations. Clients, hedge funds and trading partners rapidly pulled business or refused to extend credit amid fears over Bear Stearns’ exposure to mortgage-related securities and other hard-to-value assets.

Under the final terms, JPMorgan agreed to acquire Bear Stearns for about $10 a share in stock, a revised offer that was significantly higher than the original fire-sale price of $2 a share announced during the March crisis. The higher price helped secure shareholder approval after intense criticism from investors who argued the initial offer vastly undervalued the firm.

The transaction was made possible by extraordinary backing from the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, which agreed to finance up to $29 billion of a portfolio of Bear Stearns’ troubled assets. JPMorgan assumed the first $1 billion of potential losses on the portfolio, while the Fed’s financing was designed to shield JPMorgan from the riskiest securities and prevent Bear Stearns’ failure from rippling through the financial system.

U.S. officials defended the unusual intervention as necessary to avert a broader panic. Federal Reserve Chairman Ben Bernanke, Treasury Secretary Henry Paulson and New York Fed President Timothy Geithner said the sudden failure of Bear Stearns could have triggered severe disruptions in credit markets, given the firm’s deep ties to banks, hedge funds and counterparties around the world.

“The stability of the financial system was at risk,” officials said in various public explanations of the rescue, arguing that a disorderly bankruptcy could have produced a chain reaction across markets already strained by the housing downturn and the collapse in confidence surrounding mortgage-backed securities.

The crisis at Bear Stearns unfolded with remarkable speed. Rumors about the firm’s financial condition intensified in mid-March, prompting a rapid loss of liquidity. On March 14, JPMorgan, with support from the Federal Reserve, provided emergency funding to keep Bear Stearns operating through the weekend. Two days later, JPMorgan announced it would buy the firm in a government-supported deal.

The rescue alarmed investors and policymakers because it suggested that panic in the credit markets had spread beyond mortgage lenders and into the core of Wall Street. Bear Stearns had been a major player in mortgage securities, prime brokerage, derivatives and fixed-income trading. Its near-failure raised fears that other financial institutions could face similar pressure if counterparties lost confidence.

Markets initially reacted with turbulence, as investors questioned the health of other banks and securities firms. While the Fed’s intervention helped prevent an immediate collapse, it also sparked debate over moral hazard and whether the government had effectively extended a safety net to investment banks that were not traditionally regulated like commercial banks.

Paulson said at the time that the government’s priority was to protect the broader economy, not Bear Stearns shareholders or executives. Bernanke later told lawmakers that the Fed acted because it believed Bear Stearns’ failure would have had “severe consequences” for the financial system and the economy.

For JPMorgan, the deal brought Bear Stearns’ prime brokerage business, trading operations and Manhattan headquarters, though it also carried legal, financial and reputational risks. JPMorgan Chief Executive Jamie Dimon said the acquisition strengthened the bank’s position in key markets but acknowledged that integrating Bear Stearns would be difficult.

For Bear Stearns employees and longtime investors, the shareholder vote marked a bitter end. The firm, founded in 1923, had survived the Great Depression, multiple recessions and previous market shocks. But it could not survive the loss of confidence that swept through credit markets in 2008.

The sale is now widely viewed as one of the defining moments of the financial crisis, a warning sign of the deeper turmoil that would later engulf Wall Street.

**JPMorgan to buy Bear Stearns in fire-sale deal**

*Wall Street icon collapses after liquidity crisis; Fed backs rescue effort to prevent wider market fallout.*

**NEW YORK (CNNMoney.com) --** JPMorgan Chase agreed Sunday to acquire Bear Stearns for about $236 million, capping a stunning collapse for one of Wall Street’s best-known investment banks and marking one of the most dramatic government-backed rescues since the credit crisis began.

Under the deal, JPMorgan will pay $2 a share in stock for Bear Stearns, a fraction of the firm’s value just days earlier and far below its 52-week high. The transaction, arranged over a tense weekend of negotiations, comes after Bear was hit by a sudden liquidity crisis that left it unable to fund its daily operations.

The Federal Reserve and the Treasury Department helped broker the rescue in an effort to prevent Bear’s problems from spreading through the financial system. As part of the arrangement, the Fed agreed to provide financing support tied to as much as $30 billion of Bear Stearns’ less-liquid assets.

The deal represents a remarkable fall for Bear Stearns, founded in 1923 and long known as a scrappy powerhouse in mortgage finance, fixed income and prime brokerage. But the firm was badly damaged by the collapse of the subprime mortgage market, which triggered huge losses across Wall Street and undermined confidence in firms exposed to mortgage-backed securities.

### A crisis of confidence

Bear’s troubles intensified last week as rumors swirled that clients and trading partners were pulling business from the firm. Hedge fund customers reportedly moved cash balances elsewhere, while counterparties became increasingly reluctant to trade with Bear.

That amounted to a modern-day run on the bank. Unlike commercial banks, investment banks such as Bear Stearns relied heavily on short-term borrowing and confidence from lenders and counterparties to finance their operations. Once that confidence evaporated, the firm’s cash position deteriorated rapidly.

On Friday, Bear said its liquidity had “significantly deteriorated” in the previous 24 hours. JPMorgan, working with the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, provided emergency financing to keep Bear afloat. But that stopgap measure was not enough to restore market confidence, forcing a sale before markets opened Monday.

### Government steps in

The rescue underscores the growing concern in Washington that the failure of a major Wall Street firm could trigger broader turmoil. Bear Stearns was deeply connected to the financial markets through derivatives, mortgage securities, repo financing and prime brokerage services for hedge funds.

Federal officials faced the risk that a bankruptcy filing could lead to forced selling, counterparty losses and further panic in already fragile credit markets.

The Fed’s role in supporting the JPMorgan deal is extraordinary because Bear Stearns was not a traditional bank and did not take deposits insured by the federal government. But policymakers appeared to conclude that the systemic risks of allowing Bear to fail outweighed concerns about intervening to save a Wall Street firm.

In a separate move aimed at easing market strains, the Federal Reserve also took steps to expand liquidity available to financial institutions, part of a broader campaign to stabilize credit markets.

### A bargain for JPMorgan

For JPMorgan, the deal offers a chance to pick up Bear’s investment banking platform, prime brokerage business and Madison Avenue headquarters at a deeply discounted price. JPMorgan Chief Executive Jamie Dimon has long been viewed as one of Wall Street’s strongest operators, and his bank entered the crisis in better shape than many rivals.

Still, the acquisition carries risks. Bear’s balance sheet includes complex mortgage-related assets whose values have been difficult to determine amid frozen markets. The Fed’s financing support is intended to shield JPMorgan from some of the most troubling assets and make the transaction possible.

Bear Stearns shareholders are taking the biggest immediate hit. The $2-a-share price is a near-total wipeout compared with where the stock traded before fears about the firm’s solvency accelerated. Bear shares closed at $30 on Friday, already down sharply from more than $150 last year.

### Credit crisis deepens

Bear’s collapse is the latest and most dramatic chapter in the credit crisis that began with rising defaults in subprime mortgages and spread into nearly every corner of the financial system.

The firm had already suffered a major blow in 2007 when two Bear Stearns hedge funds heavily invested in mortgage securities collapsed. That episode was an early warning sign of the turmoil to come, as investors began questioning the value of securities tied to risky home loans.

Since then, banks and brokers have written down hundreds of billions of dollars in mortgage-related assets. Lending markets have tightened, investors have fled risky securities and central banks have repeatedly intervened to keep credit flowing.

Bear Stearns’ downfall shows how quickly a loss of confidence can destroy a highly leveraged financial institution. Even if a firm has assets that may hold long-term value, it can fail if lenders and clients refuse to provide the short-term funding it needs to survive.

### Market reaction ahead

Investors will be watching closely Monday to see whether the deal calms markets or sparks fresh worries about other financial firms. Shares of investment banks and brokerage firms have been under heavy pressure as traders question which companies may face similar funding strains.

The rescue may reduce the immediate danger of a disorderly Bear Stearns bankruptcy, but it also raises difficult questions about the health of Wall Street and the extent to which the government may be forced to intervene again.

For now, the sale ends Bear Stearns’ 85-year run as an independent firm. What had been one of Wall Street’s most storied names is being absorbed by a larger rival at a price that would have been unthinkable only a week ago.

**JPMorgan to Buy Bear Stearns in Fire-Sale Deal Backed by Fed as Wall Street Crisis Deepens**

*By [Reporter Name]*  
*NEW YORK/WASHINGTON — [Date]*

JPMorgan Chase & Co. agreed late Sunday to acquire Bear Stearns Cos. for a fraction of its value, in a fast-track rescue engineered with extraordinary support from the Federal Reserve and the U.S. Treasury after a sudden collapse in confidence left the 85-year-old investment bank unable to fund itself.

The all-stock transaction values Bear Stearns at about **$2 a share**, or roughly **$236 million**, a stunning fall for a firm whose shares traded above $150 last year and closed at $30 on Friday. The deal, negotiated over a frantic weekend with federal officials pressing for a market-stabilizing resolution before Asian trading opened, marks one of the most dramatic failures of a major Wall Street firm in modern history.

As part of the transaction, the Federal Reserve Bank of New York agreed to provide financing tied to approximately **$30 billion of Bear Stearns assets**, effectively helping JPMorgan absorb a portfolio of less liquid mortgage-related and other securities. The central bank’s intervention underscores the depth of concern in Washington that a disorderly collapse of Bear Stearns could trigger broader panic across credit markets.

“**JPMorgan Chase stands behind Bear Stearns,**” JPMorgan Chairman and Chief Executive Jamie Dimon said in a statement announcing the transaction. “This transaction will allow us to provide stability for the customers and counterparties of Bear Stearns.”

Bear Stearns Chairman and Chief Executive Alan Schwartz called the agreement the best available outcome after a rapid deterioration in the firm’s liquidity.

“**This transaction represents the best outcome for all of our constituencies based upon the current circumstances,**” Schwartz said. “We are grateful for the efforts of the Federal Reserve and JPMorgan Chase.”

## A Weeklong Collapse

Bear Stearns entered the week battling rumors about its liquidity and exposure to mortgage securities. The firm had already been badly damaged by the collapse of two hedge funds tied to subprime mortgages in 2007, an early warning sign of the credit crisis that has since spread across Wall Street.

On Wednesday, Schwartz publicly sought to reassure investors, telling television interviewers that the firm had adequate liquidity and that market speculation about a cash crunch was unfounded. But by Thursday, according to people familiar with the matter, Bear Stearns was facing a rapid withdrawal of support from trading counterparties, lenders and prime brokerage clients. Hedge funds and other customers moved to pull balances or shift business elsewhere, and short-term funding channels began to close.

By Friday morning, Bear Stearns told regulators it could not meet its obligations without emergency help. In an unusual move, the Federal Reserve and JPMorgan arranged a temporary funding facility, with JPMorgan serving as the conduit for Fed-backed financing. That action bought time but did not restore confidence.

Over the weekend, teams from JPMorgan, Bear Stearns, the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, the Treasury Department and outside advisers worked around the clock to determine whether Bear could be stabilized, sold or wound down. By Sunday evening, officials concluded that a sale to JPMorgan, backed by federal financing, was the only viable option to avoid a bankruptcy filing that could have sent shockwaves through derivatives, repo and mortgage-backed securities markets.

## Washington Moves to Contain Contagion

The Federal Reserve’s role in the transaction is highly unusual because Bear Stearns is not a commercial bank and therefore does not traditionally have direct access to central bank lending facilities. The Fed acted under emergency authority, reflecting fears that the failure of a major securities dealer could threaten the functioning of the broader financial system.

Treasury Secretary Henry Paulson, who was closely involved in the weekend discussions, said the government supported the transaction because of the risks posed by a sudden Bear Stearns failure.

“**The government is prepared to do what it takes to maintain the stability of our financial system,**” Paulson said. “The focus is on protecting the financial system and protecting the economy.”

White House officials also moved to reassure markets, emphasizing that the administration was monitoring developments but did not view the transaction as a bailout of shareholders.

“The President has been briefed on the situation and has confidence in Secretary Paulson, Chairman Bernanke and the regulators as they work to promote stability in our financial markets,” a White House spokesman said. “Our priority is ensuring that markets continue to function and that the broader economy is protected.”

The Federal Reserve separately announced new measures intended to ease pressure in short-term funding markets, signaling that it is prepared to provide liquidity to primary dealers confronting stress in the repo and securities financing markets.

## Fire-Sale Price Stuns Wall Street

The $2-a-share price is a near-total wipeout for Bear Stearns shareholders and a remarkable reversal for a firm long known for its aggressive trading culture and deep roots in fixed income markets. Bear Stearns had been one of Wall Street’s most prominent independent investment banks, with major businesses in mortgage securities, prime brokerage, clearing and investment banking.

JPMorgan said it would guarantee Bear Stearns’ trading obligations and business operations effective immediately, a critical step intended to reassure clients and counterparties before markets reopened. The company said it expects the transaction to close quickly, subject to shareholder and regulatory approvals.

For JPMorgan, the deal provides access to Bear Stearns’ prime brokerage franchise, clearing operations and Madison Avenue headquarters, but also exposes the bank to legal, credit and operational risks from a firm at the center of the mortgage-market collapse. The Fed’s financing arrangement is designed to limit some of those risks by supporting a pool of harder-to-value assets.

Dimon said JPMorgan had acted decisively because of the systemic importance of Bear’s client and counterparty relationships.

“Bear Stearns’ clients and counterparties should feel secure that JPMorgan is guaranteeing Bear Stearns’ counterparty risk,” Dimon said.

## A Defining Moment in the Credit Crisis

The rescue comes as global markets are already under severe strain from falling housing prices, rising mortgage defaults and mounting losses at major banks. Investors have grown increasingly concerned that other financial institutions may face similar funding pressures if confidence evaporates.

Bear Stearns’ collapse highlights the vulnerability of investment banks that rely heavily on short-term borrowing and confidence-sensitive funding markets. Unlike commercial banks, which are supported by insured deposits, securities firms depend on repo financing, trading relationships and client balances — all of which can disappear quickly if counterparties fear losses.

Analysts said the speed of Bear’s unraveling will force investors to reassess the stability of the remaining independent investment banks, including Lehman Brothers, Merrill Lynch, Morgan Stanley and Goldman Sachs.

“This is not just about Bear Stearns,” one senior market strategist said. “This is about whether counterparties trust the balance sheets of major financial institutions. Once that trust goes, liquidity can vanish overnight.”

## Markets Brace for Fallout

Financial markets are expected to react sharply when trading opens. The Fed and Treasury are hoping the JPMorgan transaction will calm investors by preventing an uncontrolled bankruptcy, but the fire-sale valuation may deepen concerns about hidden losses across the banking sector.

The deal also raises difficult political questions about the use of public-sector support to facilitate the rescue of a Wall Street firm. While Bear shareholders are being nearly wiped out, the Fed’s involvement places taxpayer-backed central bank resources behind a private transaction at a time when homeowners and consumers are under increasing financial pressure.

Administration officials defended the action as necessary to prevent broader damage.

“This is about systemic risk,” a White House official said. “The objective is to protect the economy, not any one company.”

For Bear Stearns employees, many of whom hold significant portions of their wealth in company stock, the deal is a devastating blow. For Wall Street, it is a warning that the credit crisis has entered a more dangerous phase — one in which even storied institutions can disappear in days if confidence breaks.

As one person involved in the weekend negotiations put it: “By Friday, there was no time left. The only question was whether Bear would open on Monday as part of JPMorgan or not open at all.”
